y-m-13-11.title: If we enlarge a square, what happen to perimeter and area?
y-m-13-11.topic: How square side and its perimeter/area change together
y-m-13-11.goal: Use examples to find how many times perimeter and area change when side multiply by a number, find rule for side factor and area factor, and explain why.
y-m-13-11.material: Doyun say, “If you double one side of a square, perimeter double and area double too.” Here square side natural number cm, area unit square centimeter (cm²).
y-m-13-11.thinking.2: Explain reason using length and width
y-m-13-11.prereq.1: Find rectangle and square area (Grade 5 level)
y-m-13-11.s.s1.prompt: Square with 3cm side enlarged to 6cm. How many times original perimeter and area each become?
y-m-13-11.s.s1.hint.0: Find perimeter and area for sides 3cm and 6cm and put in table.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.hint.1: Put original and enlarged values side by side and find factor.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.a: You confirm by calculation when side double, perimeter and area change by different factors.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.o.b: Perimeter 2 times and area 2 times too
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.b: Same as Doyun said. Calculate original area 3×3 and new area 6×6, compare.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.c: Perimeter na sum of 4 sides. Find how 12cm original perimeter change after enlarging.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.r.d: Area na length times width. Check what happen to length and width when side double.
y-m-13-11.s.s1.explain: With side 3cm, perimeter 12cm and area 9cm²; side 6cm, perimeter 24cm and area 36cm². Perimeter 2 times, area 4 times. Doyun “area doubles too” wrong for this example.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.prompt: Square side becomes k times original, its area becomes m times original. (k natural from 2 to 10.) Enter 3 different correct (k,m) pairs. You can calculate square area too.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.hint.0: Write areas for sides 1, 2, 3, 4cm in order and find how many times each change.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.hint.1: Put area factors for side factors 2 and 3 in table and find relationship between factors.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.var.k: How many times the original side
y-m-13-11.s.s2.var.m: How many times di original area be
y-m-13-11.s.s2.ok.c1: k na natural number from 2 to 10.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.fail.c1: k must be natural number from 2 to 10.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.ok.c2: When side na k times, area na m times, na correct.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.fail.c2: When side na k times, area no be m times. Try calculate am yourself.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.explain: If side na 2 times, area na 4 times; if 3 times, 9 times; if 4 times, 16 times; if 5 times, 25 times. When side become k times, both length and width become k times, so area become k×k times. Perimeter only become k times.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.prompt: Write with words di rule for how many times area become when side become k times, and explain using length and width why.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.hint.0: First write how many times length and width become when side na 2 times.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.hint.1: Use fact say multiplying length multiple by width multiple give area multiple.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You check say your rule match area multiples for both 2 times and 3 times?
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Reason why both length and width grow connect to di rule?
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.model.0: When side become k times, area become k×k times. Length become k times, and width also k times, so you multiply same number twice.
y-m-13-11.s.s2.because.model.1: When side become 3 times, area become 3×3=9 times. Length become 3 times, width also 3 times, so you multiply 3 twice.

y-m-13-04.title: Dem talk say about 800 people, but how many really dey?
y-m-13-04.topic: Estimating numbers: guessing di possible range of real number from rounded value
y-m-13-04.goal: Reason out di possible range for di real number when all you know na di rounded value, then update di range and how sure you be each time dem add information.
y-m-13-04.material: You dey find how many people use library last month. Number of users na natural number. Values wey dem write for different places fit come from different estimation methods. Rounding na method where you round up if digit just below di place wey you want na 5 or more, and round down if e na 4 or less.
y-m-13-04.thinking.0: Work out di range of real number from estimated value
y-m-13-04.thinking.1: Make di range narrower with new information
y-m-13-04.thinking.2: Decide how to judge when information no match
y-m-13-04.prereq.1: Show number ranges, like 'or more' and 'less than'
y-m-13-04.s.s1.prompt: Information go come out one piece at a time. Each time, choose wetin you think about di real number of users.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each information, first write di smallest and biggest number wey di number fit be before dem round am.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put di 2 ranges side by side on number line or list, then find where dem overlap.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Sign for library entrance talk, “Users last month: about 800 (rounded to nearest hundred).”
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin be di best ting to say about real number of users?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Natural numbers wey round to 800 for nearest hundred na 750 to 849. 750 round up to 800, and 849 round down to 800.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: E be 800 people or more and less than 900.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You think of am like range for rounding down. If you round, 790 people also become 800. 790 dey inside dis range?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Na estimated value, so you no fit say e equal real number.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: E pass 700 people and 800 or less.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You think of am like range for rounding up. Sometimes rounding go up and sometimes go down.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: E be 750 people or more and less than 850.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You turn rule “round up if lower digit na 5 or more, round down if 4 or less” into range.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Library website say, “Users last month: about 840 (rounded to nearest ten).”
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: If both information correct, wetin you fit say about real number of users?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Natural numbers wey round to 840 to nearest ten na 835 to 844. All these numbers dey inside earlier 750~849, so using both information together, real number narrow to 835~844 people.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: E be 750 people or more and less than 850. New information no change range.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You no use new information. Think about range of numbers near 840 wey round to 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E be 835 people or more and less than 845.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You keep only part where ranges from both information overlap. New information make range narrower.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You take estimated value as real number.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: E be 840 people or more and less than 850.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You think about rounding to nearest ten like rounding up or down. Wetin 836 people become when rounded?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Library guidebook give exact number, “Users: 846.” E no certain whether guidebook count users for last month.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How good to take in dis new information?
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If you no know whether guidebook count users for same month, you no fit use 846 to overturn earlier conclusion. If na same month, 846 and “about 840 when rounded” no fit both be correct, so you need check rounding method or counting period. Keeping range the same till confirmation, or deciding wetin to check and revising your thinking, both suitable.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: I no know whether na figure for same month, so I keep range 835~844 and think again after dem confirm am.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: First you check whether new information count the same thing. You keep your judgment while leaving condition to revise am.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 846 na exact count, so I decide both earlier information wrong and throw dem away.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You throw away all earlier information without even checking whether na same month.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If na same month, one of both must be off, so first I check website rounding method or counting period.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You notice new and earlier information no fit both be right, and decide wetin to check.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 846 rounded to nearest ten na 850, so I conclude website 840 wrong.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You conclude one side wrong without checking whether website round or whether na same month.
y-m-13-04.s.s1.reflect: As information come one piece at a time, how possible range change? When last information come, wetin you use to decide whether to change earlier conclusion?
y-m-13-04.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different numbers of users (natural numbers) wey fit both information (840 when rounded to nearest ten, 800 when rounded to nearest hundred).
y-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.0: Move up and down one number at a time from 840 and check whether rounded answer na 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.1: At bottom and top of range, check separately whether boundary numbers included.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Rounded to nearest ten, e na 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Rounded to nearest ten, e no become 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Rounded to nearest hundred, e na 800.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Rounded to nearest hundred, e no become 800.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.explain: Every number from 835 to 844 correct. For 835~839, ones digit na 5 or more so dem round up to 840; for 840~844, ones digit na 4 or less so dem round down to 840. These numbers also round to 800 to nearest hundred.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Write smallest and biggest number of users you fit make, and explain why na dem.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write one sentence explaining why 2 numbers at range edges different from numbers outside.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You check why 835 and 844 (or less than 845) be boundaries by checking one number outside each boundary (834, 845)?
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You write “or more / less than” correctly at range edges?
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.model.0: Smallest number na 835 people and biggest na 844. If ones digit 5 or more, e round up to 840; if 4 or less, e round down to 840.
y-m-13-04.s.s2.because.model.1: E be 835 people or more and less than 845, because 835 round up to 840 and 845 round up to 850.

y-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The three numbers na natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-13-03.title: If you put parentheses, di answer go surely change?
y-m-13-03.topic: Natural-number calculations together: parentheses and order of calculation
y-m-13-03.goal: Test di claim 'putting parentheses always changes di answer', find counterexample by yourself, and explain when di answer no change.
y-m-13-03.material: Jiho talk say, 'If you put parentheses inside expression, di answer always change.' Sua answer, 'E really dey always like that? I think say some times e no change.' Dem decide compare two expressions using three numbers a, b, c. Expression ㉮ na a + b × c (a plus b times c), and expression ㉯ na (a + b) × c (first calculate a plus b, then multiply by c). All three numbers na natural numbers 1 or greater, and dem agree to calculate multiplication before addition.
y-m-13-03.thinking.0: Understand say one example no fit decide 'always'
y-m-13-03.thinking.2: State di condition wey make am true based on wetin di examples get in common
y-m-13-03.prereq.0: Di rule to calculate multiplication first when expression mix addition and multiplication
y-m-13-03.prereq.1: Di rule to calculate inside parentheses first when parentheses dey
y-m-13-03.s.s1.prompt: When a=2, b=3, c=4, ㉮ na 2 + 3 × 4 = 14 and ㉯ na (2 + 3) × 4 = 20. From this one example, wetin you fit talk about wetin di two people say?
y-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think whether 14 and 20 support wetin Jiho talk or wetin Sua talk.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about di kind example wey you need to show say 'e dey always happen' no correct.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.a: E change one time, so I fit know say Jiho talk correct for any three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.a: You extend one example to all cases. To check 'always', you gats look at every set of three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.b: Parentheses no affect di answer, so Sua talk correct and Jiho talk wrong.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.b: You just see example where answers change to 14 and 20. Check whether this one contradict that example.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.c: If I change di three numbers some more times and di answer always change, I don prove Jiho talk.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.c: Trying a few times no be same as checking every case. Some sets of three numbers still remain wey you never try.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.o.d: You fit check wetin Sua talk only by finding at least one set of three numbers wey give equal values.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.r.d: You know say one opposite example fit disprove 'always'.
y-m-13-03.s.s1.explain: One example no fit check 'always'. You go confirm whether Sua talk correct if you find even one set of three numbers wey make both expressions equal. But to prove Jiho talk, you gats check every set of three numbers.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.prompt: Check Sua statement. Find three numbers (a, b, c) wey make a + b × c and (a + b) × c get same value, then enter dem. All three numbers na natural numbers from 1 to 20, and pairs wey only change places of a and b (for example, (1, 3, 2) and (3, 1, 2)) count as same example. You need 3 different examples.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.0: Change only one of di three numbers at a time, write both expression values, and mark when dem equal.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.1: Gather examples where both expressions get same value and look for wetin dem get in common.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c1: All three numbers gats be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Di value still equal when parentheses dey.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Di value change when you put parentheses.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.explain: For all three examples, c na 1. a + b × 1 = a + b and (a + b) × 1 = a + b, so di value equal with or without parentheses. If c no be 1, for (a + b) × c, a sef go become c times bigger, so di value go change.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Wetin di three sets of numbers wey you find get in common? Use that to write how Jiho talk suppose change.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write di three examples side by side and look for wetin dem get in common.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write one more example to show wetin happen to both expression values when that common thing change.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You check where di same part dey for all three sets of numbers wey you find?
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Jiho corrected statement accurate even without di word 'always'?
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.model.0: For all three sets of numbers wey I find, c na 1. Multiplying by 1 no change am, so e remain same with or without parentheses. So Jiho talk suppose change to 'when c no be 1', not 'always'.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.model.1: When multiplier (c) na 1, both expressions equal. For other numbers dem different, so Jiho talk correct only when multiplier no be 1.
y-m-13-03.s.s2.because.model.2: For all three examples, multiplier c na 1. So change di statement to say di answer different when multiplier no be 1.

y-m-13-12.title: If pages read double, pages wey remain go be half?
y-m-13-12.topic: Relationship where total stay same between 2 changing quantities, and checking general rule
y-m-13-12.goal: Use table and counterexamples to find mistake of extending statement wey correct for one case to all cases. Rewrite correctly di relationship wey always hold between pages read and pages left.
y-m-13-12.material: Storybook get 120 pages all together. As pages read increase, pages left decrease. Table below show pages read and pages left. When pages read na 20, 100 remain; when 40, 80 remain; when 60, 60 remain; when 80, 40 remain; when 100, 20 remain; when 120, 0 remain. Chaea look table and talk, “When pages read double, pages left become half.”
y-m-13-12.thinking.0: Find mistake in generalizing something wey correct for one case
y-m-13-12.thinking.2: Rewrite as relationship wey always hold
y-m-13-12.prereq.0: Read table and explain how 2 quantities change together
y-m-13-12.prereq.1: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication of natural numbers
y-m-13-12.s.s1.prompt: Na wetin Chaea talk to explain her statement. Read each line and choose one line wey get problem. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-13-12.s.s1.hint.0: Find how pages left change when pages read double from 20 to 40 for table.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.hint.1: Check same way from other starting page numbers in table.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.0: When pages read na 40, pages left na 80.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.1: When pages read double to 80, pages left become 40, half.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.2: So if pages read double, pages left become half.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.line.3: If you add pages read and pages left, e always be 120 pages.
y-m-13-12.s.s1.explain: Na line 3. Lines 1 and 2 match table, and line 4 also correct. But line 3 take one case, from 40 pages to 80 pages, and extend am to every starting page. If you check other starting page numbers, you go see say e no always true.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.prompt: Find case where Chae-a statement no hold. Suppose you first read x pages (x na natural number from 1 to 59), then pages read double to 2x. Let r be pages wey remain after reading 2x pages. Calculate am yourself and enter 3 different pairs (x, r) where pages left no exactly half of wetin remain first.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.hint.0: Write table with pages first read, pages left then, and pages left after reading double.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.hint.1: Compare half of pages left first with pages left after reading double, to see whether dem same.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.var.r: Pages left after reading doubled 2x pages (pages)
y-m-13-12.s.s2.ok.c1: x na natural number from 1 to 59.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be natural number from 1 to 59.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.ok.c2: Number of pages left after reading 2x pages correct.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.fail.c2: Dis different from pages wey remain after reading 2x pages. Subtract 2x pages from 120 and calculate again.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.ok.c3: When pages read double, pages left no become half. Dis na counterexample.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.fail.c3: When pages read double, pages left exactly become half.
y-m-13-12.s.s2.explain: If x=10, pages left first na 110, but after reading 20 pages, 100 remain (no be 55, wey be half). If x=20, 100 pages become 80, no be 50. Only 40 pages na exception: 80 pages left become 40.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.prompt: When x=40, Chaea statement correct. Write how you go fix her statement, including relationship wey always hold between pages read and pages left.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.hint.0: For each row of table, write sum of pages read and pages left.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.hint.1: Check again whether wetin correct for 40 pages also correct for other page numbers.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check examples (20 pages, 60 pages) to confirm say as pages read increase, pages left decrease by same amount and total stay 120?
y-m-13-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You separate case where Chaea statement correct (40 pages) from cases where e no correct?
y-m-13-12.s.s3.model.0: Even if pages read double, pages left become half only when na 40 pages. Wetin always hold na say pages read plus pages left equal 120.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.model.1: Chaea statement correct only for one case, from 40 pages to 80, and wrong for other cases. You fit say pages left decrease by as much as pages read increase, so total always 120 pages.
y-m-13-12.s.s3.model.2: Pages left decrease by exactly as much as pages read increase (for example, if you read 20 more pages, pages left also decrease by 20).

y-m-13-02.prereq.0: Find fractions wey get di same value (Primary 5 level)
y-m-13-02.title: Fractions dey between 1/3 and 1/2?
y-m-13-02.topic: Compare fractions wey get different denominators, and fractions between two fractions
y-m-13-02.goal: Check claim wey only look at denominators, make some fractions wey fit between two fractions by yourself, and confirm dem by comparing their values.
y-m-13-02.material: Ara and her friend dey talk about whether one fraction dey between 1/3 (1 over 3) and 1/2 (1 over 2). Ara: 'No natural number dey between denominators 3 and 2. So no fraction dey between 1/3 and 1/2 at all.' For here, numerator and denominator of every fraction na natural numbers.
y-m-13-02.thinking.0: Check claim wey no get reason
y-m-13-02.thinking.1: Make some fractions wey meet di conditions by yourself
y-m-13-02.thinking.2: Use comparison confirm say di fractions wey you make meet di conditions
y-m-13-02.s.s1.prompt: You wan know whether wetin Ara talk correct. Wetin you suppose do first?
y-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.0: 1/3 and 2/3 get di same denominator. Dem get di same value?
y-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think of how to change both fractions to a form wey go make you compare their values easily.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.a: Check again whether no natural number really dey between denominators 3 and 2.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.a: You dey look only at denominator size. Fraction value depend on both denominator and numerator. Even 1/3 and 2/3, wey get same denominator, get different values.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.b: Change 1/3 and 1/2 to fractions wey get same denominator, then look for fractions wey fit between dem.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.b: You use di idea say when denominators become di same, you fit compare two fractions easily by checking numerator size.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.c: Ara talk am herself, so I believe am; I no need check separately whether any fraction dey between dem.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.c: You accept am without checking di reason. One example fit disprove di statement 'no fraction dey there at all'.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.o.d: Estimate 1/3 and 1/2 as decimals and look for numbers wey fit between dem.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.r.d: Changing to decimals to compare values na useful idea too. But 1/3 decimal dey continue forever, so you need estimate am.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.explain: Even if denominators 3 and 2 dey next to each other, fraction value no depend on denominator alone. You fit check by giving both fractions same denominator and seeing whether one numerator fit enter between. You fit use decimal estimates too.
y-m-13-02.s.s1.acc.0: If you estimate with decimals, you go see number like 0.4 between 0.333… and 0.5. But 1/3 decimal dey continue forever, so you need estimate am, then change back to fraction to check which fraction e be (2/5).
y-m-13-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 fractions wey get different values, each greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2. Write fraction with numerator a and denominator b, where denominator b na natural number no more than 30. Fractions wey get same value (for example, 2/5 and 4/10) count as one.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.0: First, try one by one whether any fraction with denominator 5 dey greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.1: After you choose denominator, change numerator and check separately whether di fraction greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Numerator and denominator na natural numbers, and denominator no pass 30.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Numerator and denominator gats be natural numbers, and denominator gats no pass 30.
y-m-13-02.s.s2.explain: If you set denominator to 30, 1/3 na 10/30 and 1/2 na 15/30. Fractions between dem na 11/30, 12/30 (=2/5), 13/30, and 14/30. Other fractions like 3/7, 3/8, and 5/12 dey between dem too. Even when denominators dey next to each other, many fractions dey between two fractions.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.prompt: Choose one fraction wey you just make and write how you check say e greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2. Add one sentence wey you go tell Ara too.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write how 1/3 and 1/2 go look as fractions with same denominator.
y-m-13-02.s.s3.hint.1: Change di fraction wey you choose to one with same denominator too, then write all three fractions side by side.

y-m-13-01.title: I cross out one digit and di answer come correct
y-m-13-01.topic: Simplifying: whether di way wey dem use to make numerator and denominator simpler dey correct
y-m-13-01.goal: Use one counterexample check say getting correct answer for one fraction no mean say di method correct, and check how reliable di method be by finding fractions wey come correct by chance.
y-m-13-01.material: To write fraction 16/64 (16 over 64) in simpler way, Harin cross out digit 6 wey dey for both numerator 16 and denominator 64. Di digits wey remain na 1 for numerator and 4 for denominator, so e give 1/4 (1 over 4), and 1/4 get di same value as 16/64. Harin talk say, 'If you cross out di same digit, you fit simplify fraction.' For here, all fractions get natural numbers as numerator and denominator.
y-m-13-01.thinking.0: Know di difference between correct result and correct method
y-m-13-01.thinking.1: Test one general idea with counterexample
y-m-13-01.thinking.2: Find and check examples wey meet di conditions by yourself
y-m-13-01.prereq.0: Find fractions wey get di same value (Primary 5 level)
y-m-13-01.prereq.1: Multiply one-digit number by two-digit number
y-m-13-01.s.s1.prompt: Read Harin explanation line by line and choose one line wey get problem for di reasoning. (Line numbers start from 1.)
y-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read am and separate each line: na fact wey you fit check by calculation, or na statement wey judge say di method correct?
y-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find up to where di lines dey state only checkable facts, then check wetin di lines after that use as reason.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.0: For 16/64, cross out digit 6 wey dey both di numerator and denominator.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.1: Di digits wey remain na numerator 1 and denominator 4, so e become 1/4.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.2: 1/4 and 16/64 get di same value, because if you divide both 16 and 64 by 16, you go get 1 and 4.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.3: Di answer come correct, so di 'cross out di same digit' method sef correct.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.line.4: So for any fraction, if you cross out di digit wey dey both numerator and denominator, you fit simplify am.
y-m-13-01.s.s1.explain: Di problem dey line 4 and line 5. Up to line 3, na facts wey you fit check directly by calculation (16/64=1/4). But correct answer for one fraction no mean say di method dey always correct. Line 5 make line 4 conclusion cover all fractions, so e risky pass. Next, we go try di same method with other fractions.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.prompt: Make we try di same method with 12/21 (12 over 21). Both 12 and 21 get digits 1 and 2. (12/21 get di same value as 4/7.) Choose di correct statement.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.0: For 12/21, write wetin you get if you cross out digit 1, and wetin you get if you cross out digit 2.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.1: Use di fact say 12/21 get di same value as 4/7 compare whether each result from crossing out get di same value as 12/21.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.a: Whether na digit 1 or 2 you cross out, di result go be 2/2 or 1/1, and both equal 1, so 12/21 gats equal 1 too.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.a: You trust di result from crossing out as e be. Compare di fact say 12/21 equal 4/7 with di results from crossing out.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.b: 12/21 na only exception because e get special shape wey numerator and denominator digits change place, and di method dey always correct for other fractions.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.b: You accept one exception but still think say di method dey always correct. You don try am with other fractions?
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.c: Depending on di digit wey you cross out, e become 2/2 or 1/1, and both get different value from 12/21, so di method no dey work every time.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.c: You see say changing di digit wey you cross out change di result, and none get di same value as di original fraction. You sabi say one example fit disprove 'always'.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.o.d: If una agree say na only digit 1 for di ones place of di denominator you go cross out, e become 2/2, so di method go correct.
y-m-13-01.s.s2.r.d: You try protect di method by adding one agreement. 2/2 and 12/21 get di same value?
y-m-13-01.s.s2.explain: 12/21=4/7, but crossing out digit dey give 2/2 or 1/1, wey get different value from di original fraction. Harin method happen to work for 16/64, but e no work for 12/21. One counterexample disprove di claim say 'this method dey work for every fraction'.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.prompt: Make we find fractions wey Harin method work by chance. Think of fractions wey numerator na two-digit number ab (a na tens digit, b na ones digit) and denominator na two-digit number bc (b na tens digit, c na ones digit). If you cross out di same middle digit b, you go get a/c. Enter 2 fractions apart from 16/64 where a/c after crossing out get di same value as di original fraction. a, b, and c na digits from 1 to 9, and a and c dey different.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write a/c yourself, then multiply numerator and denominator by di same number to check whether e get di same value as (10a+b)/(10b+c), di original fraction.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.1: Set b to 9 and check by changing a and c one after another.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.var.b: Digit b to cross out (di numerator ones digit and denominator tens digit)
y-m-13-01.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, and c na digits from 1 to 9.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c1: a, b, and c gats all be digits from 1 to 9.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c2: If a and c be di same, e go be like 11/11, wey already get value 1, so we no include am.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c3: You don see 16/64 before. Find another example.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.ok.c4: Di fraction before crossing out and a/c after crossing out get di same value.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.fail.c4: Di fraction a/c after crossing out get different value from di original fraction.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.explain: We get 19/95 (=1/5), 26/65 (=2/5), and 49/98 (=1/2). If we add 16/64, na only four such fractions dey. For most fractions, crossing out digit dey change di value. So apart from cases wey work by chance, crossing out digits no be method wey you fit trust.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.prompt: After searching, you find say na few such fractions dey. Write wetin you wan tell Harin about di method of crossing out digits.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.hint.0: Think of one example like 12/21 where crossing out give wrong answer.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.hint.1: Think about how few fractions you find, then check whether di word 'always' correct.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Your reason include one clear example, like 12/21 or one fraction wey you find?
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: You write say 'di method correct' and 'di answer happen to be correct dis time' no be di same thing?
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.model.0: Harin method happen to work for some fractions like 16/64, but e no dey always work. For 12/21, di value change depending on which digit you cross out, and e no match 4/7 too. Use di method of dividing numerator and denominator by di same number.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.model.1: Di answer happen to be correct by chance. Na few such fractions dey, like 19/95, 26/65, and 49/98. Most ones like 12/21 give wrong answer, so no trust crossing out digits.
y-m-13-01.s.s3.because.model.2: Harin, di method of crossing out di same digit dey almost always wrong, and e work by chance for only very few fractions.

y-m-13-05.title: 5/6 + 3/8: compare 4 methods
y-m-13-05.topic: Adding fractions: compare different ways to add 2 fractions with different denominators
y-m-13-05.goal: Among several methods to find sum of 2 fractions with different denominators, pick methods wey fit work, and make examples explaining when 2 correct methods same and when dem differ.
y-m-13-05.material: You wan add 5/6 (5 over 6) and 3/8 (3 over 8). Four friends each suggest different method. One say add numerators 5+3=8 and denominators 6+8=14 to get 8/14. Another say make denominator 6×8=48 and calculate 40/48 + 18/48. Another say make denominator 24, common multiple of 6 and 8, and calculate 20/24 + 9/24. Last friend think 5/6 about 0.83 and 3/8 about 0.38, so sum about 1.2.
y-m-13-05.thinking.0: Compare whether different solution methods valid
y-m-13-05.thinking.1: Make your own cases where 2 methods differ
y-m-13-05.thinking.2: Explain strengths and weaknesses of methods with words
y-m-13-05.prereq.2: Find common multiples of 2 numbers (Grade 5 level)
y-m-13-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all methods wey fit find exact fraction value of 5/6 + 3/8.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write what form each method change di 2 fractions into, and check whether denominators become same.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether result from each method bigger or smaller than 5/6 by itself.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.a: Add numerators and denominators to get 8/14.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.a: If you add denominators, size of each piece change, so you no longer count pieces of same size. Compare whether 8/14 bigger or smaller than 5/6.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.b: You use idea of changing both fractions to same size pieces before adding.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.c: Estimate 5/6 and 3/8 as decimals and say sum about 1.2.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.c: Estimate tell you roughly di value, but e no give exact fraction. E useful for checking.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.o.d: Make denominator 24, common multiple of 6 and 8, and add.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.r.d: You choose smaller common multiple to keep numbers small.
y-m-13-05.s.s1.explain: If you make denominator 48 or 24, you turn both fractions into same size pieces and add, so sum same (58/48 = 29/24). 8/14, from adding numerators and denominators separately, even smaller than 5/6, so e no fit be sum. Estimate no be exact value, but you fit use am to check whether calculation correct.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 denominator pairs (p, q) where method of multiplying denominators and method using smallest common multiple give different denominators. Like 6 and 8, p and q na natural numbers from 2 to 12, and p smaller than q.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.hint.0: Find product and smallest common multiple of 2 denominators, then write dem side by side.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write separately denominator pairs where product and common multiple same, and pairs where dem differ. Find di difference.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q na natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c2: p must be smaller than q.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.ok.c3: Product and smallest common multiple different.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.fail.c3: Product and smallest common multiple same, so both methods give same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s2.explain: For 6 and 8, product na 48 but smallest common multiple na 24, so dem different. Same for 4 and 6 (product 24, common multiple 12) and 4 and 12 (product 48, common multiple 12). For 2 numbers wey no get common divisor apart from 1, like 3 and 5 or 5 and 7, product na smallest common multiple, so both methods give same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.prompt: You fit get right answer by multiplying denominators, but write wetin convenient about using smallest common multiple. Also give one pair of denominators where both methods give same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.0: For 6 and 8, write denominators wey you get from each method.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.1: From your s2 results, choose denominator pairs where both methods gave same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: For 2 denominators you use as example, you find product and smallest common multiple yourself and check whether dem same?
y-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You explain “convenient” clearly, like say less calculation?
y-m-13-05.s.s3.model.0: If you use smaller common multiple, numerators and denominators smaller, so calculation easy, and at di end you no need simplify as much. Two denominators like 3 and 5, where only 1 fit divide both, get product equal to smallest common multiple.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.model.1: If you use product of denominators, numbers get bigger, so calculation long and you fit need more simplification at di end. When product itself na smallest common multiple, like 5 and 7, both methods give same denominator.
y-m-13-05.s.s3.model.2: If you use lowest common multiple, you fit add smaller fractions, so calculation easier. If denominators get no common factor apart from 1, like 3 and 5, both methods same.
